verdicts.trueWording: the format says you should have a “Tactics” section, so you might as well write two or three paragraphs about it
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched by curl (browser UA, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in the 'Adventure Formatting Guides' section: the format 'tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”' and the orcs/swords example supplies the 'nothing needed saying' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it should talk about the ogre first
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the raw page; the very next clause supplies the hidden-goblin limb: 'a room with a goblin hiding behind a tapestry, on the other hand, shouldn’t lead off with the goblin.' Alexander frames it as 'the problem… of sequencing information'.

verdicts.trueWording: the culmination of this approach is the infamous “delve” format … the rigid adventure format forces information to be presented out-of-sequence
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim and the 'culmination of rigid formatting' limb is supported ('This sort of one-size-fits-all formatting becomes both a straitjacket and an excess. And the culmination of this approach is the infamous “delve” format'). But the page never ties the delve format to 4th Edition: its only edition markers are '2nd Edition' (Apocalypse Stone) and 'When 3rd Edition arrived'; grep for '4th'/'fourth' on the page returns nothing, and the delve discussion is deferred to another article ('which I’ve talked about extensively elsewhere').
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the page never identifies the delve format as fourth edition's

verdicts.trueWording: Boxed text is usually not a good thing.
verdicts.note: Verbatim bullet inside the list under the page's own heading 'Review Standards / Bryce Lynch / What I’m looking for in an adventure module may not be what you are looking for.' Attribution limb ('his own list') confirmed by that framing.
Verbatim bullet in the same Bryce Lynch 'what I’m looking for' list, two bullets after 'Evocative atmosphere.'
Verbatim bullet (with the period) in Bryce Lynch's own list on the raw page.

verdicts.trueWording: I don’t care about your epic backstory. Give me a little to work with to get things going.
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe matches). The second sentence on the page supplies the 'only enough to start play' limb.

Verbatim. It sits in the scale under the separate 'The Pretty Girl' section, whose author writes 'not the gourmand that Bryce is' and 'When I built my rating scale'; 4 is the top of that Language scale (4/2/1/0). The phrase is absent from Bryce's own bullet list, so the negative limb holds. Attribution is by section heading rather than a literal sign-off.
Verbatim, including the space after the slash; it is the 0 rung, the lowest of the same 'The Pretty Girl' Language scale (4/2/1/0).

verdicts.trueWording: I LOATHE the overly long backstory and fiction intro’s, but they are not on this list.
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the comments, attributed 'Bryce Lynch says: April 19, 2016 at 8:36 am' — date and 'fiction introductions' limb both confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the article's third sentence. The cited /36903/ URL 301-redirects to /35180/roleplaying-games/the-art-of-the-key (verified with curl url_effective); both fetches returned the identical page, md5 191eaa61f9514f5b28703a6167ef75ee.

verdicts.trueWording: boxed text — prewritten text designed to be read aloud by the GM
verdicts.note: Verbatim appositive in 'The Era of Boxed Text' section; it is Alexander's definitional gloss, exactly as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: In either 1979 or 1980, depending on how persnickety you want to get with definitions
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the same sentence names 'Lost Tamoachan: The Hidden Shrine of Lubaatum' as where boxed text 'arrived for the first time'. Note the page later hedges further, giving Quest of the Fazzlewood (1978) an 'honorable mention' that 'one could argue… is, in fact, the first example' — an extra caveat, not a contradiction of the claim's two limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it should talk about the ogre first
verdicts.note: Verbatim; Alexander introduces it as 'that of sequencing information', and the hidden-goblin counter-example confirms the sequencing-by-what-is-met-first limb. Same sentence as index 635.

verdicts.trueWording: Instead of making the information easy to parse and reference, a rigid format ends up having the opposite effect.
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and it is the closing sentence of Part 1 immediately before 'Go to Part 2'. The stated aim ('easy to parse and reference') is in the same sentence, so both limbs hold.
